title: If people knew
hookLine: if beings knew the fruit of giving, they would not eat without sharing (Itivuttaka 26)
last: SUMANA — GLAD BEFORE, BRIGHT DURING, HAPPY AFTER.

lines: THE LAST SLICE IN THE BOX.
cards: One slice of pizza left in the box. Four people around the table. Everybody saw it.

Nobody's reaching. A tiny standoff, polite and a little ridiculous, until someone finally says, go on, split it? Now the same slice at midnight, alone in the kitchen: it's simply gone, no thought at all.
The Buddha said something about that last bite, a line so strong it can sound almost impossible. It's in a small book of his sayings, and it opens with a condition: if people knew.

teach.b: The book is the Itivuttaka, which means this was said: short teachings the tradition remembers as the Buddha's own words.

teach.h: IF THEY KNEW THE FRUIT OF GIVING.
teach.b: In saying twenty-six, he says, in substance: if beings knew, as I know, the result of giving and sharing, they would not eat without first giving. The stain of stinginess would not take hold of their minds.

Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat it without sharing, if there were someone to share it with. But because they don't know, they eat without giving, and stinginess stains their minds.
Notice what this teaching isn't. It isn't a rule: you must share. It's a claim about knowledge.
The problem isn't that people are bad.

teach.h: NOT A COMMAND, A WAY OF SEEING.
teach.b: It's that they don't see what giving actually does. If they could, sharing would be as obvious as stepping out of the rain. So what does giving do?
The texts talk about good results in this life and future lives. But they also point to something anyone can check tonight.
The saying calls stinginess a stain, and it can sit in the body as something tight and small. Sharing loosens it. Back to the last slice.
When someone splits it, the whole table relaxes. Nobody got much pizza. Everybody got something better.
And look at the words: the last bite. Not the leftovers, not what you didn't want. Sharing the last of something is where generosity stops being easy and starts being real.

how: Some Buddhists set aside part of a meal to offer first, at a home shrine, to monks or to guests, and sharing food is an everyday form of dana.

o: saving part of a meal for later
sharing, dividing out what you have
a fair trade of goods between people

games.q: match the piece of today's saying.
p: still shared, if someone is there

s: the saying is a rule: you must share
it's a claim about knowing: if beings knew the fruit of giving, they would share.
the saying mentions even the last bite, the last mouthful
even then, they would not eat without sharing, if someone were there.
the Itivuttaka's name means 'this was said'
it's a collection of short sayings remembered as the Buddha's own.

games.q: according to the saying, why do people eat without sharing?
o: because they don't know the fruit of giving.
games.why: the saying puts it down to not knowing: if they saw what giving does, sharing would be obvious.

practice: Think of something you usually keep to yourself: the last cookie, the good seat, the end of the coffee, an hour of quiet. Imagine giving it away, and if a little tightness comes, don't fight it; just feel where it sits in the body.
Then picture yourself sharing it anyway, and the other person's surprise, and notice what happens to the tightness.

wordCard.voice: Samvibhaga. Sharing, dividing out: the Buddha's saying that if beings knew the fruit of giving, they wouldn't eat even their last bite without it.

orig.note: Pali: sharing, dividing out; the saying speaks of giving and sharing (dana-samvibhaga).

carryVoice: Your line: share the last bite. Stinginess is a stain, and sharing loosens it. Day one hundred thirty-four, done.
